newsitem.title: USA: US drillers see rates firm but little new capacity.
newsitem.headline: US drillers see rates firm but little new capacity.

text.p: Firmer dayrates for oil rigs and full contract books are cheering the oil and gas drilling industry but even at these improved levels, new capacity is thin on the ground and likely to remain so.

"We have our order books full for all jackups and floaters outside the Gulf of Mexico, while in the Gulf rig rates have been rolling over at better rates for the past year," said David Herasimchuk, vice president in charge of marketing at Global Marine Inc.

A jackup, which is attached to the seabed floor, is generally used to drill in shallow waters while a floater, or submersible rig, is not attached to the ocean floor and used for deeper water drilling.

Most other drillers say contracts expiring in the second quarter have been rolled over at higher rates but the recent bust from which the industry is recovering means that repair and conversions are more likely than building.

Global's smallest jackup in the Gulf of Mexico commands dayrates in the mid-$40,000 dollars but that would have to rise to $60,000 to make new capacity worthwhile, for a semi-submersible rig like its Global Arctic III, which would cost $220 million to build, dayrates of $170,000 would be required compared with the current $135,000-$140,000.
Instead, companies are converting hulls and upgrading and lengthening the life of existing capacity.

"This industry fell very hard, almost every company went through a reorganization and you have a generation of managers which is very leery of building," said Robert Fulton, chief financial officer at Falcon Drilling Co Inc.
Wall Street also seems unsure how to treat the sector, which has retreated from all-time highs in January.
Last week, the sector rallied for a couple of days on the record Gulf of Mexico lease sale and then fall back as investors focused on the prospect of weaker energy prices.
The S&P Oil Drilling Index rallied 1.27 percent on Monday to 3,157 points, still off its January 15 high of 3,430.
"What we see are short-term investors who are very sensitive to the earnings outlook for these stocks, which produces share price volatility," said one company spokesman.
The industry and some analysts believe the short-term is overdone and the longer-term earnings prospects remain intact.

"What people fail to realize is that we are at the start of a multi-year recovery for the drilling industry. Capital spending by exploration and production companies is strong and that is what drives demand," said Salomon analyst Mark Urness.
In the North Sea, rates are closer to the level at which new capacity becomes feasible.
Transocean Offshore Inc has a $290 million drillship on order for 1998 with an initial drilling reach of 7,000 feet and the potential for an upgrade to 10,000.

"The work that is coming off the coast of Norway and runs west of the Shetlands and down off the coast of Ireland is all lightly explored and requires a floater that has to do much more than just drill deep, it has to survive in a harsh environment," said Jeffrey Chastain, head of investor relations at Transocean.
Last week's record lease round in the Gulf of Mexico will also create demand but industry executives caution it will be some time before that becomes work for the drillers.

"This will require additional equipment to get drilled and some may be upgraded, some may be conversions and some may be new, but the impact is going to be far out in to the future," said Global Marine's Herasimchuk.
One way of increasing capacity has been to buy, but that has become more expensive as share prices and rates rallied.
"We do continue to look at opportunities, in the past we were aggressive when you could buy for cents on the dollar, now the business has turned, that is much more difficult," said Falcon's Fulton.
In the end, new capacity may come from the exhaustion of the plant which is working flat out.
"The rate at which these rigs are drilling may be the final factor in deciding whether there is new capacity as they wear out," said Fulton. ((-- New York Newsroom +1 212 859 1902))
